unit.title: Gear and clothing
unit.summary: Why hikers carry what they carry: the ten essentials, layering, feet and packs.

lessons.title: The ten essentials
lessons.objective: You can list the ten essentials as systems and say what problem each solves.

payload.prompt: Why is a headlamp part of the ten essentials on a morning hike?

options.text: For unplanned delays that push you past dark
options.explanation: Delays, injuries, wrong turns and slower partners add hours to your plan.

options.text: To see better in bright sunlight
To scare off animals at night
Most trails require one by law

explanation.correct: Plans slip. A headlamp is cheap insurance that turns a late finish from an emergency into just an inconvenience.
explanation.incorrect: No one plans to be out after dark, which is exactly why the light lives in the pack. It is the smallest, cheapest safeguard.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I always throw a headlamp in my pack. Better to have it and not need it."

payload.prompt: Match each essential to the problem it solves.

pairs.definition: Map, compass and GPS to find your way when the trail is unclear
Sunscreen, sunglasses and hat to prevent burn and heat illness
Extra layers to survive an unplanned night or cold weather
Headlamp and backup so you can travel safely in darkness
Bandages, tape, pain relief and tweezers for cuts, blisters and splinters

distractorDefinitions: A device to track how far you have gone

explanation.summary: The ten essentials are really ten systems, each solving a different hazard. Knowing why you carry them matters as much as packing them.
explanation.sayThisLine: "The essentials cover the main ways things go wrong."

payload.prompt: Which is NOT one of the ten essentials?

options.text: Fire starter
Repair kit and tools
A full-size tent
Extra food

explanation.correct: A full tent is too heavy for day hiking. The essentials ask for emergency shelter like a bivy or space blanket.
explanation.incorrect: Fire, repair, food and water are all on the list. They are small, light and critical.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Emergency shelter means a bivy, not a full tent."

payload.prompt: Complete the essential.
payload.template: Your {{item}} is the system for treating {{hazard}}, so small problems stay small.

explanation.correct: First aid covers cuts, sprains, allergies and blisters. A repair kit (knife, tape, cord) fixes gear.
explanation.incorrect: First aid and repair are separate systems. First aid is for your body, repair is for your gear.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: For a short trail I still pack the full ten. Some people think I'm paranoid.

options.text: It is smart to be prepared for something going wrong
The ten essentials are a reasonable pack weight even for short hikes
That is overkill for a short trail
Carrying them shows irrational fear

payload.translation: She prepares for emergencies on even short hikes. The ten essentials are lightweight insurance.

followUps.line: What essentials are smallest to pack?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about the items themselves.

followUps.line: Have you ever actually needed one?
followUps.why: Invites a story about when prep paid off.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking what the essentials are is totally fine if you are not sure.

payload.prompt: A friend is hiking a well-traveled one-mile trail to a lake. Should they carry the ten essentials?

scene.alt: A short, popular hiking trail on a sunny day.

choices.label: No, it is too much for short hikes

explanation.correct: Accidents happen on short trails too, and help can take a while to arrive even on a popular one. A twisted ankle, wrong turn or weather change is easier to handle with the essentials.
explanation.incorrect: The essentials are light enough to always carry. Even a short, busy trail can leave you waiting for help longer than you would think.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Even a short trail can go wrong. The essentials are light enough to always carry."

lessons.title: Layers, not a big coat
lessons.objective: You can build a layering system and say what each layer does.

payload.prompt: Match each layer to its job.

pairs.definition: Thin, wicking fabric against skin that pulls sweat away
Insulating fleece or down that traps warm air
Outer wind and rain barrier that vents so you do not sweat inside it

distractorDefinitions: A thick cotton coat that keeps you warm

explanation.summary: Three layers, three jobs. A base wicks, a mid insulates, a shell sheds weather. You add or peel off layers as temperature changes.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Base, mid, shell. I add or remove them as I go."

payload.prompt: Order the steps to build a good layering system for a cool autumn hike.

items.text: Start with a wicking base layer against your skin
items.why: Moisture against skin leads to chilling fast.

items.text: Add a mid layer of fleece or wool for warmth
items.why: Insulation needs to be over the base.

items.text: Wear a shell on top for wind and water protection
items.why: The shell goes last so weather does not reach the insulation.

items.text: Adjust by adding or removing the mid layer as you warm up or cool down
items.why: The mid layer is the easiest to peel off.

explanation.correct: Building from skin out, wicking first, insulation middle, shell last, lets you adjust as you go.
explanation.incorrect: The order matters. Base layer first stops moisture, mid layer keeps you warm, shell last keeps weather out.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I dress in layers so I can adjust without stopping."

payload.prompt: Why do hikers wear layers instead of one thick jacket?

options.text: So they can adjust to temperature changes without stopping
Three thin layers weigh less than one thick one
It looks better
Parks require you to wear layers

explanation.correct: Temperature on trail changes with exertion, elevation and time of day. Layers let you stay comfortable without stopping.
explanation.incorrect: One thick jacket traps you in sweaty discomfort or shivering cold. Layers adapt as conditions change.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I peel off layers as I warm up from climbing, then put them back as I cool down at the top."

payload.prompt: Complete the guidance.
payload.template: Your mid layer should be {{material}} because it insulates even when {{condition}}.

explanation.correct: Wool and fleece hold much of their warmth even when damp. Cotton soaks up water and loses most of its insulation.
explanation.incorrect: Synthetic and merino wool are far better than cotton for hiking. You want insulation that works when things get damp.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: I wore one heavy wool sweater and it was perfect until I got to the top and cooled off. Then it was unbearable.

options.text: One thick piece does not let you adjust
A thick sweater is harder to pack and carry
One heavy sweater is better than layers
Wool is the wrong material

payload.translation: A single heavy layer traps you in too hot or too cold. Layers give you choices.

followUps.line: Did you pack the sweater out or tie it to your pack?
followUps.why: Explores the practical problem of carrying a puffed-up sweater.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is fine to ask how layering works if you are new to it.

payload.prompt: Cool drizzle is forecast. Which top do you reach for?

scene.alt: Two options shown as words only: a heavy cotton hoodie and a synthetic shell layer.

explanation.correct: Synthetics shed water and dry fast. Cotton soaks in rain and holds moisture against your skin, chilling you rapidly.
explanation.incorrect: Cotton stays wet for hours and drains heat once you stop moving. A synthetic shell sheds rain, and wicking layers under it manage sweat.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Cotton is a no in drizzle. Synthetic or wool layers, always."

lessons.title: Why cotton is the villain
lessons.objective: You can explain why cotton is a poor choice in cool or wet weather.

payload.prompt: For a cool, rainy day hike which shirt is better?

scene.alt: Two t-shirts shown as words only: a cotton t-shirt and a merino wool or synthetic base layer.

explanation.correct: Synthetics and wool wick sweat away and dry quickly. Cotton absorbs moisture and drags heat from your body.
explanation.incorrect: Cotton stays soaked for hours. When you stop moving, that wet layer chills you fast. Hypothermia can happen above freezing in wet cotton.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Cotton kills. Synthetic or wool, that is the rule."

payload.prompt: Why do hikers avoid cotton even on cool, dry days?

options.text: Cotton holds sweat against your skin instead of wicking it away
Cotton is heavier than synthetics
Cotton smells worse after a day on trail
Modern hikers just do not wear cotton anymore

explanation.correct: Wicking pulls sweat off your skin to the outer surface where it evaporates. Cotton traps sweat against skin, leading to chilling.
explanation.incorrect: Even on cool days, you sweat on climbs. Cotton holds that moisture and can chill you when you stop or cool down.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Even on a cool day, cotton traps sweat. Wicking fabric lets it evaporate."

payload.safetyNote: Hypothermia can occur in temperatures well above freezing, especially with wet clothing.
payload.prompt: Cold rain at 8,000 feet. Cotton sweatshirt soaked. Change or continue?

situation.narrative: You are exposed at altitude wearing a heavy cotton sweatshirt that is now wet from rain. You have synthetic layers in your pack.

facts.label: Backup gear
facts.value: Synthetic base layer and shell in pack

options.label: Stop and change into your synthetic base layer and shell
options.consequence: Synthetics wick sweat and shed rain. Within a few minutes you should start to warm up. Keep moving, eat something, and watch for shivering that will not stop.
considerations: Cotton loses most of its insulation when wet
Wind and wet multiply the chilling effect
Hypothermia risk rises fast in these conditions

options.label: Keep the cotton on and push on
options.consequence: Wet cotton keeps you in direct contact with cold. Shivering, clumsiness and confusion build over the next hour.
considerations: Wet cotton conducts heat away from your body
Even at 55 F, hypothermia is possible in wind and wet
Stopping to change takes minutes, not hours

options.label: Keep moving faster to generate more heat
options.consequence: Activity warms you momentarily, but you sweat more, making the wet cotton worse. Exhaustion follows.
considerations: Exercise does not overcome wet cotton against your skin
You can not keep moving fast forever
The cold is not the enemy, the wet is

payload.expertNote: Hypothermia can happen fast in wind and wet, even above freezing. Cotton loses most of its warmth when soaked. Change into dry synthetics now, not later.
payload.sayThisLine: "If I feel cold in cotton, I change out of it. Now, not after another mile."

payload.prompt: Match the fabric to what it does when you sweat.

pairs.definition: Wicks moisture away from skin so it dries fast
Wicks sweat and keeps some insulation even when damp
Absorbs water and holds it against your skin, then dries very slowly

distractorDefinitions: Keeps you warm by trapping sweat in a protective layer

explanation.summary: Wicking means pulling sweat away so it can evaporate. Cotton does the opposite, trapping water.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Wicking keeps you dry and warm. Cotton does the opposite."

payload.prompt: Complete the safety rule.
payload.template: On any hike, avoid {{avoid}} because when it gets wet it {{consequence}}.

options: dries slowly and loses most warmth
gaps.correct: dries slowly and loses most warmth

explanation.correct: Cotton holds water and stops insulating. Wind and cool temperatures can then drop your body temperature dangerously fast.
explanation.incorrect: Cotton is a hazard in the backcountry because it does not wick sweat and dries very slowly.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: I wore jeans on a hike once and got drenched. My legs were freezing by the end.

options.text: Cotton denim holds water and stops insulating
That is a lesson learned about choosing fabrics
That was just bad luck with the weather
Jeans are fine for hiking

payload.translation: Cotton soaked, lost its insulation value, and left them chilled. The right fabric matters.

followUps.line: Would synthetic pants have changed that day?
followUps.why: Shows you get the cause and effect.

followUps.line: Do you carry spare pants now?
followUps.why: Invites a story about lessons learned.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Everyone makes the cotton mistake once. Asking why fabrics matter is smart.

lessons.title: Shoes that fit
lessons.objective: You can explain why fit beats brand and how to check it.

payload.prompt: What matters most in choosing hiking shoes?

options.text: Proper fit beats brand, price or what others use
Buy the most popular brand, everyone wears it
The most expensive shoe is always best
Tall boots always prevent ankle sprains

explanation.correct: Wrong fit ruins even great shoes. Your foot should lock at the heel, have room for toes to spread and not slide on descents.
explanation.incorrect: Fit is personal. Wrong-size boots from any brand cause blisters and pain. The right shoe for your foot is the right choice.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Fit matters more than brand. Wrong size ruins your day."

payload.safetyNote: Poor footwear fit can cause blisters, pain and lead to dangerous falls on difficult terrain.
payload.prompt: New boots slide on descents. What is the problem?

situation.narrative: You fitted new hiking boots at a store. The fit felt okay. On a practice hike the next day, your foot slides forward inside the boot on descents.

facts.label: Store fit test
facts.value: Heel felt snug, toe-to-box spacing one finger-width

options.label: Try a heel-lock lacing and retest on a real descent
options.consequence: A heel-lock lacing pins the heel and often stops the slide. If your foot still slides, or your toes bang the front, get refitted for size and shape before a long hike.
considerations: Lacing is the free first fix
Test on a real descent in hiking socks
Still sliding means the boot may be the wrong size or shape

options.label: Return them and try a half size smaller
options.consequence: If the boot really is too big, a smaller size can lock the heel. But with a finger-width already at the toe, smaller may crowd your toes. Have a fitter check it.
considerations: Sliding can mean too big, or just loose lacing
A too-small boot jams toes on descents
Get a professional fit check

options.label: Try a different brand that fits better
options.consequence: Different brands have different lasts. A different brand might fit your foot shape better, but this brand in a smaller size might also work.
considerations: Fit is personal, not brand-specific
Try a smaller size in this boot first
Brand switching is an option if size does not fix it

payload.expertNote: Feet slide forward on descents when the heel is not locked. Better lacing, socks, or a different size or shape can fix it. Fit boots in the socks you will wear and test them on a slope.
payload.sayThisLine: "My foot slid on the downhill, so I tried heel-lock lacing and got the fit checked."

payload.prompt: Complete the fitting rule.
payload.template: In proper hiking boots, your heel should {{heel}} and your toes should {{toe}}.

options: have about a finger-width of room
touch the inside of the toe box
gaps.correct: have about a finger-width of room

explanation.correct: A locked heel prevents sliding on descents. A finger-width of toe room lets your toes splay and swell without hitting the front.
explanation.incorrect: Heel lock is essential for stability and blister prevention. Too-tight toes cause blisters and pain quickly.

payload.prompt: Match the fit problem to what it causes.

pairs.definition: Foot slides forward on descents and heel moves inside the boot
Toes jam the front and go numb, blisters form on the toes
Heel locked, finger-width toe room, soles feel solid on rough ground

distractorDefinitions: Brand affects fit more than personal foot shape does

explanation.summary: Size, heel lock and toe room are non-negotiable. Fit matters more than price, brand or what anyone else wears.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I try boots on and hike in them before deciding. Fit is everything."

payload.prompt: Which boot shows a good fit?

image.alt: Three side-view boot fits shown: one where the heel slides loose, one where toes jam, and one where heel is locked and toes have room.

options.text: Left: heel slides, toes have room
Center: heel locked but toes jam
Right: heel locked, toes have a finger-width of room

explanation.correct: Heel locked and toe room: that is the fit that works. The center is too tight, the left is too loose.
explanation.incorrect: A loose heel slides on descents and causes blisters. Jammed toes cause pain and numbness. Look for the boot that locks the heel and gives toe room.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Heel should be snug, toes should have room. That is a good fit."

cues: Heel stays in place with minimal movement
Toes have about a finger-width of space

statement.speaker: Morgan
statement.text: I bought the exact brand and model a friend has, but my feet hurt. Turned out we have different foot shapes.

options.text: Foot shape varies, so the same shoe fits differently on different people
Fit is personal, brand does not matter as much as fit
That friend gave you bad advice
That brand is the wrong choice

payload.translation: Great boots on her feet might be painful on yours. What matters is fit for your foot.

followUps.line: Did you find a shoe that works better for you?
How do you decide what boots to try now?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking how to know if a shoe fits is a great question.

lessons.title: Blisters before they happen
lessons.objective: You can treat a hot spot early and know the order of care.

payload.prompt: Order the response to a hot spot.

items.text: Feel warmth or friction on your heel
items.why: That tenderness is the signal to act right now.

items.text: Stop and take off your shoe and sock
items.why: Do not push through friction. Stopping early prevents a full blister.

items.text: Dry and clean the area with a cloth
items.why: Tape does not stick to damp skin.

items.text: Apply tape or a blister pad over the hot spot
items.why: Reduces friction so it never blisters.

items.text: Change socks if wet and re-lace your boot snugly
items.why: A snug heel lock prevents slipping and rubbing.

explanation.correct: Stopping early with dry skin and tape prevents most blisters. Do not skip the drying step or tape will fall off.
explanation.incorrect: Tape on wet, unstopped friction fails. Stop first, dry thoroughly, tape, then re-lace snugly.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Hot spot? Stop and tape it before it blisters. Stop early, stop often."

payload.prompt: You feel a hot spot at mile three. What do you do?

options.text: Stop immediately and tape it before it blisters
Keep walking, it will go away
Tape it at lunch, it is not urgent
Ignore it, moleskin works better on full blisters

explanation.correct: A hot spot is your last chance to prevent a blister. Five more minutes of friction and it becomes a fluid-filled blister that ruins your hike.
explanation.incorrect: Stop now. Continuing over a hot spot guarantees a blister. Tape early is far easier than treating a full blister.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I stop for hot spots. Five more minutes and it is a blister I have to hike on for hours."

payload.safetyNote: Keep a blister clean and covered. See a clinician for spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever.
payload.prompt: Quarter-sized blister on heel. How do you treat it now?

situation.narrative: You have a fluid-filled blister on your heel, about the size of a quarter. You are midway through a six-hour hike and have a sterile pad and blister pack in your first aid kit.

facts.label: Gear available
facts.value: Sterile pad, moleskin, blister pack in kit

options.label: Cover with a sterile blister pad or donut pad to cut the pressure
options.consequence: The pad removes friction. The blister stays intact and protected. You finish the hike with manageable pain.
considerations: An intact blister is less likely to get infected
Pressure relief is the main thing that helps
Keep it clean and change socks

options.label: Drain it now to relieve pressure
options.consequence: The fluid drains, but the wound is now open to bacteria and dirt. The risk of infection rises and it stays painful.
considerations: An open blister is an infection risk
Pressure relief does not require popping it
Covering works as well without the risk

options.label: Leave it alone and keep hiking
options.consequence: Three more hours of rubbing on a full blister. By the end, the skin around it is shredded and the whole area is raw.
considerations: Ignoring a full blister makes it worse
The friction keeps building
A pad takes two minutes to apply

payload.expertNote: A full blister needs protection from friction, not popping. Cover with a sterile pad or moleskin donut and you can finish your hike.
payload.sayThisLine: "I cover a blister with a pad, keep it clean and change my socks. No popping."

payload.prompt: Complete the prevention rule.
payload.template: A hot spot is friction turning into heat; the key is to {{action}} before it becomes {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Tape a hot spot the moment you feel it. Another mile of friction and you have a blister.
explanation.incorrect: A hot spot is friction and heat. Tape stops the rubbing and prevents a blister that would be painful for the rest of your hike.

payload.prompt: Match the blister stage to the right care.

pairs.definition: Warm, tender friction: stop and tape immediately to prevent a blister
Cover with a sterile pad or moleskin donut to remove pressure
Keep clean and covered with a sterile pad to prevent infection

distractorDefinitions: Pop blisters to drain them faster

explanation.summary: Catch friction early as a hot spot, tape it, and avoid blisters. If a blister forms, cover and protect it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Tape hot spots. If a blister forms, keep it clean and covered."

statement.speaker: Riley
statement.text: I ignored a hot spot for another mile. By the time I stopped to tape it was already a blister.

options.text: The lesson is to tape hot spots immediately, not wait
Pushing through teaches you what you can handle
Some people just get blisters
That was bad luck with your boots

payload.translation: One extra mile of friction turned a preventable hot spot into a blister. Stop early.

followUps.line: How long did the blister slow you down?
followUps.why: Invites a story about the cost of waiting.

followUps.line: Do you tape hot spots now?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Admitting you ignored a hot spot is honest. Everyone learns this the hard way once.

lessons.title: Packs and poles
lessons.objective: You can choose a sensible daypack size and explain what poles do on descents.

payload.prompt: What is a good size for a day-hiking pack?

options.text: 10 to 30 liters, depending on your trip length
50 liters or more to carry extra gear
Less than 10 liters, minimal weight
Size does not matter, any pack works

explanation.correct: A 10 to 30 liter daypack fits food, water, layers and emergencies. Too small and you skip essentials; too large and you overpacked.
explanation.incorrect: Oversizing your pack tempts you to carry gear you do not need. A right-sized pack carries the essentials without excess weight.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I use a twenty-liter pack for day hikes. Enough for essentials and snacks."

payload.prompt: Which pack is right-sized for a day hike?

image.alt: Three packs shown from front: an oversized 60-liter mountaineering pack, a well-fitting 20-liter daypack with hip belt, and a tiny 5-liter sling.

options.text: Left: large mountaineering pack
Center: compact daypack with hip belt
Right: tiny sling pack

explanation.correct: The center pack fits the day hike essentials with a hip belt to carry load on your hips, not shoulders.
explanation.incorrect: The left is overkill for a day hike. The right is too small for food, water and layers. The center pack is right-sized.
explanation.sayThisLine: "A daypack with a hip belt carries your gear without straining your shoulders."

cues: Padded hip belt to distribute weight

payload.prompt: What do trekking poles do for you on a descent?

options.text: They reduce load on your knees by distributing impact
They let you hike faster downhill
They improve balance on steep or rocky ground
They make you look like an experienced hiker

explanation.correct: Poles transfer some impact from your knees to your arms and shoulders. Over thousands of downhill steps, this saves your knees.
explanation.incorrect: Poles do not make you faster, but they do let you hike longer descents by reducing the stress on your knees.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Poles save my knees on descents. Without them my quads are shredded the next day."

payload.prompt: Complete the gear setup.
payload.template: A {{size}} daypack keeps your load manageable, and {{poles}} on descents reduce strain on your {{joint}}.

explanation.correct: Right-sized packs and poles work together to keep you comfortable and capable.
explanation.incorrect: A daypack that is right-sized carries necessities without excess weight. Poles on descents protect your knees from repetitive impact.

payload.prompt: After a long descent your knees ache for days. Should you try trekking poles next time?

scene.alt: A steep downhill trail seen from above.

choices.label: Yes, poles reduce the impact on knees
No, poles are only for steep mountains

explanation.correct: Poles distribute downhill impact across your arms and shoulders, saving your knees. They help on any descent, not just steep mountains.
explanation.incorrect: Poles help on any sustained descent. If your knees hurt after hikes, poles can make a real difference.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Poles made a huge difference in my knee pain. I use them on every descent now."

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: I brought a huge backpack to day hikes at first. Now I use a smaller one and feel so much better.

options.text: A right-sized pack matches your trip, not your gear
Carrying less weight for hours makes a big difference
Bigger packs mean you are more prepared
Pack size is not that important

payload.translation: Right-sizing the pack to the trip lets you hike longer and feel better.

followUps.line: What size pack do you use now?
How does it feel to hike lighter?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking what pack size is right for you is a totally smart question.

lessons.title: Light, shelter and sun
lessons.objective: You can explain why a day hiker carries a headlamp, a bivy and sun protection.

payload.prompt: Complete the sun safety rule.
payload.template: UV rises with {{altitude}} and reflects off {{surfaces}}, so you need {{protection}} even on cool days.

explanation.correct: High elevation and reflective surfaces like snow raise your UV exposure a lot. Sunburn happens fast in the mountains.
explanation.incorrect: Cool temperatures do not mean low UV. Sunburn at altitude is painful, and clouds do not block all of it.

payload.prompt: Why does a day hiker carry an emergency shelter like a bivy or space blanket?

options.text: For an unplanned night out due to injury or getting lost
So you can camp anytime you want
It is heavier than your other layers combined
Parks require it

explanation.correct: A twisted ankle, wrong turn or darkness can trap you out overnight. A bivy or space blanket is light, small survival insurance.
explanation.incorrect: You hope to never need it, but an unplanned night happens. A tiny bivy or space blanket weighs ounces and can save your life.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I carry a space blanket the size of a deck of cards. I hope I never need it."

payload.safetyNote: UV is stronger at altitude and off snow, and can burn you quickly even on cool, cloudy days.
payload.prompt: Above treeline, cool and cloudy. Time for sunscreen?

situation.narrative: You are above treeline at 10,000 feet on a cool, cloudy afternoon. The sky is gray and you feel chilled. You have sunscreen in your pack.

options.label: Apply sunscreen now
options.consequence: Clouds do not stop most UV, and altitude makes it stronger. Five minutes now, plus a hat and sunglasses, prevents a bad burn.
considerations: Clouds block heat but not most UV
UV is stronger at altitude
Snow and rock reflect UV upward

options.label: Skip it, you are not that cold
options.consequence: The cool weather lulls you into ignoring UV. By evening you are burned red across your face and ears. The burn gets worse over two days.
considerations: Temperature is not the same as UV risk
Sunburn at altitude happens fast
It does not hurt while it is happening

options.label: Wait until it clears up
options.consequence: The clouds thin without clearing. You are still getting hit with UV but do not realize it. Sunburn builds before you react.
considerations: Do not wait for perfect conditions
Cloudy days can still burn you badly
Above treeline is always high risk

payload.expertNote: Altitude and reflection raise UV exposure. Cool cloudy days fool people into skipping sunscreen. Above treeline, protect your skin and eyes.
payload.sayThisLine: "Clouds do not stop most UV at altitude. I wear sunscreen even on cool, gray days."

payload.prompt: Match the essential to why it matters.

pairs.definition: Hands-free light so you can travel safely if your hike runs past dark
Tiny bivy or space blanket for surviving an unplanned night
Sunscreen, sunglasses and hat because UV is stronger at altitude and reflects

distractorDefinitions: A full sleeping bag for car camping

explanation.summary: These three protect you from darkness, cold and sun damage. All three are light and all three can save your day.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Light, shelter and sun protection. Even for a short hike, I carry all three."

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: I got a terrible sunburn above treeline in spring. The snow reflected so much UV I did not realize it was happening.

options.text: Snow and water reflect UV and increase your exposure
That is a hard lesson about altitude and reflection
That was just unlucky timing
Sunburn is not a big deal

payload.translation: High altitude plus reflective snow created dangerous UV. Sunscreen and protection are non-negotiable above treeline.

followUps.line: Do you apply sunscreen now even on cool days?
How long did the burn last?
followUps.why: Invites a story about the consequences.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is totally normal to underestimate altitude UV. Everyone learns this lesson eventually.

payload.prompt: You are hiking a three-mile loop that should take two hours. Should you bring a headlamp?

scene.alt: A short, well-traveled hiking loop on a clear day.

choices.label: No, it is a short daytime hike

explanation.correct: Delays, mistakes and slower partners add hours. A headlamp is lighter than a chocolate bar and worth the space.
explanation.incorrect: No one plans to hike after dark. A headlamp is small insurance for a plan that slips.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I take a headlamp on every hike. It weighs nothing and has saved me more than once."

lessons.title: First aid and repair
lessons.objective: You can sketch a sensible first aid and repair kit for a short hike.

payload.prompt: What belongs in a basic first aid kit for day hiking?

options.text: Bandages, blister pads, tape, pain reliever and tweezers
A full emergency trauma kit like paramedics carry
Supplies for treating every possible injury
Nothing, you can get help if needed

explanation.correct: A day hiker's first aid kit covers blisters, cuts, splinters and minor sprains. Keep it light and tailored to your training.
explanation.incorrect: Carry what you know how to use. Blisters and scrapes are the common issues on day hikes.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My first aid kit weighs ounces. Bandages, tape, antibiotic ointment and pain reliever."

payload.prompt: Match the kit to what it solves.

pairs.definition: Bandages, tape, antibiotic and pain relief for cuts, blisters, sprains and allergic reactions
Knife or multi-tool, cord, duct tape and safety pins to fix gear on the trail
Waterproof matches or a lighter for warmth or signaling in an emergency, where fires are allowed

distractorDefinitions: A surgical suite in a backpack

explanation.summary: First aid is for your body, repair for your gear, fire for emergencies. All three are light and part of the essentials.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Duct tape wrapped on a pencil fits your pocket and fixes almost anything."

explanation.correct: Keep it small and focused on common issues. A lightweight kit is one you will actually carry.
explanation.incorrect: An oversized first aid kit stays home. A small one fits in your hip belt and makes the hike.

payload.translation: Gear breaks on trail. A couple of ounces of tape and cord can save a day.

followUps.line: What else do you carry for repairs?
Has the repair kit helped you before?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Carrying a simple repair kit is smart planning, not paranoia.

payload.prompt: Should you carry a first aid kit on a short, well-traveled, popular trail?

scene.alt: A well-marked and popular day-hiking trail.

choices.label: Yes, blisters and cuts happen everywhere
No, popular trails have rescue nearby

explanation.correct: Blisters, scrapes and splinters happen on any trail. A light first aid kit means you can treat small issues and keep hiking.
explanation.incorrect: Rescue is for emergencies, not blisters. Self-treatment with a basic kit keeps small problems from ruining your day.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Even on a popular trail I carry first aid. Blisters do not care how busy the trail is."

payload.safetyNote: Bleeding that will not stop with firm pressure is an emergency: call for help. Check that your tetanus shots are current.
payload.prompt: Small cut from rock scramble. How do you treat it?

situation.narrative: You scraped your palm on a rock during scrambling. It is a small cut with a little bleeding, but it is dirty and exposed. You have water, antibiotic ointment and bandages.

facts.label: Contamination
facts.value: Dirt and rock dust in the wound

options.label: Rinse with water, apply antibiotic ointment and cover with a bandage
options.consequence: The cut is clean and covered, which keeps infection risk low. Watch it over the next few days.
considerations: Rinse out dirt with clean water
Cover it to keep it clean
See a clinician for spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever

options.label: Leave it open to air so it dries faster
options.consequence: Dirt stays in the wound, and sweat and friction keep it damp. It is more likely to turn red, swollen and infected.
considerations: Dirt is an infection source
Backcountry wounds are at high risk
Covering is the correct first aid response

options.label: Ignore it, it is too small to matter
options.consequence: Two hours of dirt exposure and friction. The wound may swell and redden by evening and could become infected.
considerations: Small cuts can infect as easily as large ones
Trail dirt is not clean
Prevention takes minutes, treatment takes days

payload.expertNote: Clean, ointment, cover. Small backcountry cuts can get infected, so keep an eye on them. Bleeding that will not stop under firm pressure is an emergency.
payload.sayThisLine: "Small cuts treated now do not turn into infected sores later. I clean and bandage every one."
